spec.title: Should AI companies get an antitrust exemption to slow down?

claims.text: On The Verge's Decoder podcast, Nilay Patel talks with Jonathan Kanter, the former antitrust chief at the US Department of Justice under President Biden.
evidence_terms: former antitrust chief for the US Department of Justice

claims.text: The CEOs of major AI labs have asked for antitrust exemptions so they can coordinate on safety issues.
Critics see regulatory capture, or even a cartel forming.
Kanter's view is that this powerful technology needs basic rules of the road.

scenes: Wide studio shot. The presenter sits at the desk and looks into the camera as a lower-third graphic reads 'Decoder: AI and antitrust'. The Verge headline appears as a floating card to the right.
Close-up on the presenter speaking. An on-screen graphic lists three words stacked vertically: 'Exemption', 'Coordination', 'Safety', each highlighting in turn as she speaks.

Side-view medium shot. The presenter gestures toward a graphic that shows two labels, 'Regulatory capture' and 'Cartel', with a question mark between them, then the graphic fades to a road with lane lines being drawn in.
spec.script: Here is a question you might not expect: should AI companies be allowed to coordinate with each other? On The Verge's Decoder podcast, Nilay Patel talks with Jonathan Kanter, the former antitrust chief at the US Department of Justice under President Biden. The backdrop is the debate over AI safety, where the CEOs of major labs have asked for antitrust exemptions so they can coordinate on safety issues. Critics see something else: regulatory capture, or even a cartel forming. Kanter's view is that this powerful technology needs basic rules of the road. You decide who should be writing them.
